passages.text: Quantization-aware training (QAT) is the most reliable way to obtain accurate low-bit large language models (LLMs), but training with AdamW keeps two dense FP32 states for every weight matrix. We find that low-rank memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore and LDAdam degrade substantially in QAT. A considerable part of the QAT momentum lies outside its top- r r singular subspace, and projection-based methods discard this part at every step. We further observe that this residual remains useful when only its sign is kept. Based on these observations, we propose ResQAdam. It keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the r × r r\times r coordinates of the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update computed from the residual. We evaluate ResQAdam with two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, with weights quantized down to 2 bits. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%. Our code is available at https://github.com/LiqunMa/ResQAdam .
We compare ResQAdam with AdamW in from-scratch QAT and QAT fine-tuning, in terms of training loss, final perplexity and accuracy, and optimizer-state memory.

Optimization Trajectory and Convergence Alignment. As illustrated in Figure 2 , ResQAdam closely tracks the training-loss trajectory of the dense AdamW baseline. Across all evaluated bit-width configurations and both frameworks, the training loss curves of ResQAdam closely overlap with the baseline from initialization through to the final iterations. The zoomed-in callouts at the end of the training horizons further highlight that ResQAdam maintains stable convergence without divergence. This confirms that our geometry-decoupled and space-specific update strategies sufficiently capture the quantization errors to stabilize the low-bit pretraining process. Curves for the 200M model are in Appendix B . Language Modeling Quality. Table 1 reports the final validation perplexity across model scales and quantization settings. For both QuEST and CAGE, ResQAdam achieves perplexities close to full-state AdamW, with several cases where ResQAdam is slightly better. These results show that ResQAdam largely preserves AdamW-level language modeling quality in from-scratch QAT while substantially reducing optimizer-state memory.

Total peak memory is defined as the maximum GPU memory consumed during training, encompassing weights, activations, gradients, and optimizer states. All experiments utilize the Basic QAT framework with a W4A4G128 quantization configuration and a context length of 4096. Training is conducted on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU. The micro-batch size is set to 1 with 128 gradient accumulation steps. ResQAdam uses a uniform projection rank of r = 64 r=64 . The reported optimizer-state memory strictly accounts for the transformer backbone and excludes the embedding and language modeling head layers.

As detailed in Table 3 , ResQAdam consistently reduces the optimizer state footprint by over 71% across 3 different LLMs. This efficiency directly translates to a 15.3% to 19.5% reduction in total peak memory. This substantial memory reduction incurs minimal computational overhead. The training throughput decreases by less than 2% compared to standard AdamW in all evaluated cases. These results show that our amortized update strategy substantially alleviates the optimizer-state memory bottleneck of QAT while maintaining competitive training throughput.

Table 4: Perplexity comparison of memory-efficient optimizers under diverse QAT paradigms and quantization configurations. Projection-based optimizers use rank 64. For a fair comparison, all optimizers are tuned with a grid search over learning rates, and the best result is reported. Low-rank projection methods such as GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) and LDAdam ( Robert et al., 2024 ) restrict adaptive states to a rank- r r subspace obtained from the gradient, with LDAdam adding state transport across changing subspaces and error feedback. Structural factorization methods such as AdaFactor ( Shazeer and Stern, 2018 ) keep the full parameter dimensionality but approximate the second moment by row and column statistics. Table 4 reports the average perplexity on WikiText-2 and C4. In from-scratch QAT, every baseline is far behind ResQAdam in both quantization settings, by a margin much larger than the differences we observe between ResQAdam and AdamW in Table 1 . This is consistent with our hypothesis that confining the update to a low-rank subspace, or replacing the second moment by a factorized approximation, loses part of the correction that QAT relies on. In fine-tuning the picture depends on the bit width. At W2A16G128 the projection-based methods remain clearly behind, whereas at W4A4G128, where quantization error is small, all optimizers land within a narrow range and the choice of optimizer matters little.

passages.text: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. We study how optimizer geometry and depth jointly govern this behavior through a common framework for singular mode dynamics. Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. To highlight, SignGD and ideal Muon eliminate the divergent birth barrier and drive unsupported modes to zero in finite time. Cumulative Shampoo initially retains GD’s depth-dependent barrier, then accumulated gradients produce a catch-up phase while making previously active modes increasingly persistent. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced slowdown while preserving the ordering of the target singular values, whereas positive damping introduces a spectral threshold below which the slow GD phase laws reappear. These results give normalization, accumulated state, damping, and depth a direct interpretation as controls determining when modes emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

Saxe et al. (2013) derive exact learning dynamics for deep linear networks under structured initial conditions, including a decoupled mode representation and equal strengths across layers. (2018) show that linear overparameterization changes the effective optimization geometry and can act as a preconditioner. Du et al. (2018) study balancing properties of gradient flow in homogeneous models, while Arora et al. Some of the representative approaches include adapter modules ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , prefix tuning ( Li and Liang, 2021 ) , prompt tuning, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. 2022 ). Among these, LoRA stands out as an attractive option because it keeps the pretrained backbone frozen and modifies selected linear maps by adding trainable low-rank updates. More formally, for a weight matrix W 0 ∈ ℝ m × n W_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} , LoRA parameterizes the adapted weight as W = W 0 + T , T = U ​ V ⊤ , U ∈ ℝ m × r , V ∈ ℝ n × r , W=W_{0}+T,\qquad T=UV^{\top},\qquad U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}, The rank r r is typically chosen by the practitioner as a hyperparameter rather than something derived from the fine-tuning objective itself ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Schulman and Lab, 2025 ) . passages.text: To validate the effectiveness of our preconditioning 5 for LoRA, we conducted LoRA fine-tuning experiments on natural language generation, image classification, and commonsense reasoning tasks, following the existing LoRA studies [ 21 , 63 , 56 , 41 , 26 ] . All experiments were performed in PyTorch [ 42 ] on a single H100 GPU with 80 GB VRAM. We downloaded the pre-trained models using Hugging Face Transformers library [ 57 ] .

Following [ 21 , 63 ] , we conducted LoRA fine-tuning for the GPT-2 medium model [ 45 ] on E2E natural language generation challenge task [ 38 ] , which assesses the fine-tuned model’s ability to generate fluent and semantically accurate sentences from meaning representations. We followed the same experimental setup as in [ 63 ] , except that we tuned the learning rate over { 0.02 , 0.04 , … , 0.30 } \{0.02,0.04,\dots,0.30\} for SGD and { 0.0002 , 0.0004 , … , 0.0030 } \{0.0002,0.0004,\dots,0.0030\} for AdamW methods on the validation set. For all methods, we inserted the low-rank matrix B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} into the query and value matrices of the attention layers in the GPT-2 model. This motivates a minimal method ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After): During an initial phase, ORCA applies a soft orthogonality penalty, R orth ​ ( 𝐖 ) = 1 4 ​ ‖ 𝐖𝐖 ⊤ − 𝐈 ‖ F 2 R_{\mathrm{orth}}(\mathbf{W})=\frac{1}{4}\|\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{\top}-\mathbf{I}\|_{F}^{2} . Then directly removes it at a single switch point. Training thereafter follows the standard optimizer update, with no gradual decay or further changes. This design lets early regularization influence the optimization path without prescribing the spectrum throughout training. In our experiments, this simple release is followed by faster loss reduction and a lower final validation loss than Muon. Figure 1.1: LLaMA 130M training dynamics. Effective rank is measured on a middle-layer V V projection; the dashed line marks regularization release. Figure 1.1 illustrates the transition. While the penalty is active, the effective rank of the weight matrix rises sharply above Muon’s, although ORCA initially has a higher validation loss. After release, the rank falls from its peak but remains above Muon’s, while validation loss decreases rapidly, crosses the Muon curve. The result is consistent with early spectral shaping leaving a useful effect on the subsequent trajectory, even after the explicit penalty is gone. Controlled interventions in Section 5 further investigates into this connection.

We evaluate ORCA on LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained MoE models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, including 100B-token training runs. ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon across these settings. In most experiments, the reduction is 0.02–0.04, comparable to or greater than Muon’s gain over Adam. To put this loss reduction in perspective, on LLaMA 1.3B, ORCA achieving the 0.024 lower validation loss reaches Muon’s 100k-step loss in just 60k steps. Further, downstream evaluations, alternative early spectral interventions, multi-seed runs, and ablations of method parameters and intervention timing further support these gains. Together, these results show that early spectral shaping followed by constraint relaxation can improve training efficiency and final performance across architectures without substantial changes to the optimizer. To summarize the contributions of the paper: (1) We illustrate a trade-off in spectral control through a simplified model and empirical observations: favorable spectra can accelerate optimization but persistent constraints may harm the attainable solution quality. (2) We introduce ORCA, a minimal shape-then-release optimizer that leverages early orthogonal regularization to improve optimization trajectories while allowing unconstrained adaptation in later training. (3) We demonstrate ORCA’s effectiveness across diverse LLM architectures and scales, achieving faster convergence and lower loss than existing optimizers. Through extensive controlled experiments, we further validate the mechanism that early effective-rank shaping drives the observed improvements.

passages.text: MapHub, the MIDAS arXiv Preprint Hub, assesses each day’s new arXiv submissions for every participant in a research community, with a large language model reading each paper against portfolios built for the participants. It publishes the relevance scores, from 0 to 100, as a heatmap that shows whose work each paper touches. In the authors’ blind ratings, the top 10% of papers by MapHub’s scores held about 70% of the raters’ own top 5%, pooled, against about a third for a text-matching baseline. About 6% of a day’s astro-ph papers reach 30 for each participant, and one every three days reaches 60. MapHub runs on a standard Claude subscription and is designed to be useful for any field: https://github.com/kailicao/maphub-public .

Nowadays, each arXiv announcement brings about ninety new astro-ph submissions, and readers cannot attend to all of them equally [ 4 ] . myADS runs keyword and author queries on new preprints [ 5 ] ; recommenders learn a reader’s interests from topics, text similarity, or ratings [ 6 , 3 ] , or adapt inspectable profiles day by day [ 8 ] . Open-source projects use large language models to rank each day’s listing against one reader’s interests, and at Ohio State, agents built from 21 faculty members’ publication records each discuss matching daily papers [ 7 ] . These tools serve one reader at a time, or share discussions, rather than publishing how each paper relates to each member. MapHub 1 1 1 https://kailicao.github.io/maphub-public/ combines three things: Every new paper is scored for every participant and shown in one heatmap, one row per paper and one column per participant; the profiles are portfolios that participants can check and correct themselves; the scores are public and traceable.

A public prompt can be used to draft each participant’s research portfolio from a publication record, and the participant checks it: about 1,500–3,000 words, built from their own papers and plans, listing methods and targets as well as topics. Portfolios stay among participants and the model’s provider; scores are public, as participants agree when they join. Claude Opus 5.5 [ 1 , at low effort;] reads each new paper’s title, authors, and abstract against the portfolios and returns a relevance score from 100 (“the participant wrote the paper, or would”) through 60 (“would cite it”) and 30 (“it may broaden their view”) to 0, a fit to the portfolio rather than a judgment of quality. MapHub assesses new submissions to its listings (here astro-ph and cs.AI; the listings can be configured). Since most cells score low, a first pass scores chunks of about 50 papers for all participants at once against short outlines of the portfolios, and only papers scoring 10 or more are rescored against a full portfolio. On two test listings (748 papers), this cost about 36% of a single full pass and missed none of the 56 cells that pass scored 40 or more. The prompts, code, and tables are public, scores are labeled as AI-generated, and each table’s commit records what produced it, so the output can be checked. Figure 1: (a) An example day of MapHub, as its viewer shows it: the 23 papers (of 262) that reached 30 for some participant on 2026 August 25, numbered by average score. (b), (c) The share of each rater’s top 5% (b) and top 15% (c) found, against the share of astro-ph papers read in order of score. Columns are pooled and weighted back to uniform sampling; bands are 68% bootstrap intervals.

Seventy listings scored with version 0.8’s portfolios and prompt held 11,932 new submissions, scored for one individual, two groups, and two collaborations. Of a day’s 87 astro-ph papers, 6.3 % ± 3.5 % 6.3\%\pm 3.5\% (mean ± \pm standard deviation) reach 30 for each participant and 0.4% reach 60. Even the individual column, spanning multiple subfields, sees only 7 ± 3 7\pm 3 astro-ph papers a day at 30 or more: minutes of reading abstracts. And 8% of astro-ph papers reach 30 for two or more participants (Figure 1 a). Of a day’s 84 cs.AI papers, about two reach 30 for the individual, and almost none for the others. To test whether the scores save time, the authors rated one shared list blind for themselves or their groups on MapHub’s rubric, each interpreting its descriptions in their own way. 2 2 2 One rater recast its descriptions as a scale from 1 to 5. Only each rater’s order is used. The list held 45 astro-ph papers drawn with probabilities rising with a paper’s highest score ( ∝ 2 s / 20 \propto 2^{s/20} ), five of them shown twice, and 10 cs.AI papers spanning the individual column’s scores. Papers by the participants were left out; the portfolios were fixed on 2026 October 14 and cite none of the rated papers. Each rating is weighted by the inverse of its paper’s chance of being drawn, so the results estimate what reading these listings would find. A paper counts as of interest if it is in the rater’s top 5% (or 15%) of the population by their own ratings.

Reading in MapHub’s order finds the rater’s top 5% quickly (Figure 1 b): MapHub’s top 5% of papers hold about a third of it, and its top 10% about 70%, against 33% for a term-frequency baseline (TF-IDF 3 3 3 https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.feature_extraction.text.TfidfVectorizer.html of title and abstract against the portfolio) reading the same share. MapHub’s lead is 39 points at 10% read (95% interval: 11–60; ahead in every bootstrap draw). The top 15% is spread more widely: MapHub’s top 10% holds about a third of it, against about 20% for TF-IDF, and the two converge when about 40% of the listing is read (Figure 1 c). MapHub’s cutoff of 30 means reading 4%–9%, and over 90% of the papers above it were in the rater’s top 15%.

A department’s heatmap could help an Astro Coffee-style discussion 4 4 4 https://astronomy.osu.edu/coffee of the whole listing: Papers touching several columns are natural topics, and their highest-scoring participants natural people to ask. Portfolios drawn from publication records may miss interests not yet published: The groups’ portfolios name machine learning only as a tool for their science, so MapHub may miss AI papers their members want. Adding these interests to the portfolios would fix this; meanwhile, the individual’s column flags AI papers. Scores stay comparable across days, since every paper is read against the portfolio on one rubric, and rescoring changed them by 1.7 points on average. MapHub is still under development, and the test is small. Its ratings are subjective: The first author, who built the tool, rated three of the five columns, and a rating shifts with the papers read just before it. Each rater’s top 5% holds few papers, and defining interest by percentile assumes every rater has some.
